prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and of its active form, which made incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part prize for B002 naming Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The first round showed that all six of us reached the same configuration by separate routes, but I do not count that as an argument. The argument is that this is a specific discovery that visibly changed a field: the incretin effect and proglucagon processing, the truncated active peptide, the receptor biology, and then therapies whose benefit in type 2 diabetes, obesity and cardiovascular and renal disease has been confirmed in large independent outcome trials over roughly two decades. The mechanism is clear and the interpretation has been stable for long enough that the impact is no longer a prediction. The committee has also now tested the alternatives. B001 has the most severe attribution crowding on the list and a clinical payoff that is still early. B035 lacks the original chimeric-receptor concept among its credited names and bundles Rosenberg's adoptive cell transfer with CAR design, which are related but different steps. Neither is cleaner than B002, and I do not see a second distinct achievement that earns a place beside it this year, so I keep one part.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the weakness and I have not resolved it. Priority for identifying and characterising the active GLP-1 peptide is contested between Mojsov, the Habener group and Holst. I cannot verify it from the material I am permitted to use, and I will not pretend that the round-1 discussion settled it. Habener is outside the credited names, and a three-person cap means any trio omits someone with a credible claim. Excluding Knudsen is a choice with a cost: the long-acting analogue design is what produced liraglutide and semaglutide, and a critic can say the prize honours the idea but not the medicine. Part of the impact is industrial, which sits awkwardly with a discovery prize. If the primary record shows that Mojsov's contribution to the active form is weaker than the supplied evidence suggests, the third slot has to be reopened.

responses.point: Sandberg moved from a Drucker, Holst and Knudsen trio to the shared discovery trio, and states that this is a judgement under the three-person cap and not a finding that Knudsen's contribution is minor.
responses.response: I agree that the record should say exactly that, and I would put it in the committee's written reasoning, not leave it implicit. In round 1 I was sceptical of Knudsen's claim, and Linnarsson's point that turning a peptide with a half-life of minutes into a once-weekly drug took real scientific invention has made me less comfortable with a dismissive framing. I still keep Mojsov in the slot, because the identification and synthesis of the active peptide is the step the whole development rests on. My reasoning is about framing, not about which contribution was harder. If the evidence on Mojsov proves weak, I would accept Knudsen in that slot and a citation that says plainly the emphasis has moved from discovery to translation. I do not accept your argument that the Mojsov dispute lowers B002 relative to the alternatives. I agree with you there, since the alternatives have equal or worse attribution problems.

responses.point: Svenningsson says the omission problem cannot be fixed by adding names under the cap, only by wording the citation narrowly enough that it claims no more than these three did, so that Habener and others are not implicitly written out.
responses.response: I accept this and have changed my citation accordingly. My round-1 wording spoke of the physiology of GLP-1 and its active form. The revised wording says discoveries of the physiology of GLP-1 and of its active form, which made incretin-based treatment possible. That claims discoveries by these three without asserting that they alone identified the peptide or that no one else contributed. I also agree that excluding Knudsen must be defended on its merits and not by calling her work industrial. The defence I would give is that the prize recognises the discovery that made the drugs conceivable, while the analogue chemistry is development built on it. I recognise that this is a judgement and that reasonable members could draw the line elsewhere. On your question of a single or two-part prize, I would keep one part, because no second achievement in our shortlist has a cleaner credit than B002.

responses.point: Linnarsson says he would reconsider the third name if the Mojsov evidence proved weak, and that Sandberg's Knudsen configuration would then be his fallback.
responses.response: I share that conditional, and I think it is the honest position, since none of us has seen the primary record and the chair has asked the secretariat to check. My difference from you is on what would trigger it. A contested priority claim is not by itself a reason to drop a name. The question would be whether the documented work on the active peptide, as opposed to the dispute about emphasis, supports crediting her. If it does, I would keep her even though Habener's claim is real and unaddressed. I also take your correction on my earlier characterisation of Knudsen, and I will not describe her contribution as merely development. For the fallback ordering I agree with El-Manira rather than with your opening order, in that I would place B035 only marginally ahead of B001 because the missing Eshhar concept is a gap in the credited list, while B001 needs an arbitrary cut among six names. I list both and do not regard either as comfortable.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius would rather phrase the citation to cover the development arc than displace a discoverer, and says the active-form identification is the step that made GLP-1 a usable therapeutic idea.
responses.response: I agree with the principle that a discoverer should not be displaced just to cover development, and with your preference for working this out in the citation. My caution is that a citation cannot do much about the cap. Wording that gestures at long-acting analogues without crediting the person who designed them would claim recognition we have not given. I would rather be explicit that the citation covers the physiology and the active form, and state in the record that analogue design is outside this prize's credited achievement. I differ with you in one respect. You treat the active-form step as what made GLP-1 therapeutically usable, but that is the part whose priority is contested, so I would hold that claim loosely until the primary record is checked. I also agree with your view on B035, that Rosenberg's role is a distinct step, and with your reluctance to put it forward as a co-recipient.

uncertainties: Who identified and characterised the active truncated GLP-1 peptide first, and whether the primary record supports Mojsov's share against the Habener group and Holst. I have not verified this and the discussion so far has not either.
Whether the committee can word the citation so that it claims what Drucker, Holst and Mojsov did without implicitly writing out Habener or Knudsen.
Whether excluding Knudsen is the right judgement or whether the committee will, on reflection, treat the long-acting analogue design as part of the discovery.
Which of B001 or B035 is the better fallback if B002 stalls on credit, given that each needs an allocation that omits someone with a credible claim.
Long-term safety and durability of benefit for incretin therapies, which are still being characterised, though I do not think they undercut the core discovery.
statement.conflict_note: No documented involvement with any credited name on a shortlisted ballot. I worked with Ronald Evans on nuclear receptors during my time at the Salk Institute, but he is not credited on any shortlisted ballot. I have co-authored with Per Svenningsson and once with Abdel El Manira (2009); these are general collaborations unrelated to B002, B001 or B035, and I do not request recusal. My research field (nuclear receptors, dopamine neurons) touches optogenetics only by topic and I have tried to discount that. This is unchanged from round 1.
